title: Can, must, want
goal: Master three helper verbs that unlock hundreds of new sentences: asking permission, expressing obligation, and saying what you want.
bekal: say what you have to do with *devo*
turn down and accept invitations gracefully

dialogs.title: Dialogo — Non posso, devo lavorare
dialogs.intro: Marco invites Budi over. Budi has to say no — and saying no politely is a skill of its own.

lines.speaker: Marco:
lines.text: Budi, stasera vuoi venire a cena da noi?
lines.id: Budi, do you want to come to dinner at our place tonight?
lines.literal: Budi, tonight you-want to-come to dinner from us?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Vorrei tanto, ma non posso. Devo studiare.
lines.id: I'd love to, but I can't. I have to study.
lines.literal: I-would-like much, but not I-can. I-must to-study.

lines.speaker: Marco:
lines.id: Come on, you can study tomorrow!

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Domani devo lavorare tutto il giorno. Ho un esame venerdì.
lines.id: Tomorrow I have to work all day. I have an exam on Friday.
lines.literal: tomorrow I-must to-work all the day. I-have an exam friday.

lines.speaker: Marco:
lines.text: Va bene, capisco. Possiamo fare sabato?
lines.id: OK, I understand. Can we do Saturday?
lines.literal: goes well, I-understand. we-can to-do saturday?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Sabato sì, volentieri! A che ora devo venire?
lines.id: Saturday, yes, gladly! What time should I come?
lines.literal: saturday yes, gladly! at what hour I-must to-come?

lines.speaker: Marco:
lines.text: Verso le otto. Non devi portare niente.
lines.id: Around eight. You don't need to bring anything.
lines.literal: toward the eight. not you-must to-bring nothing.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Can I at least bring the wine?

lines.speaker: Marco:
lines.text: Se vuoi. Ma davvero non devi.
lines.id: If you want. But you really don't have to.
lines.literal: if you-want. but truly not you-must.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Voglio portare qualcosa. È la mia educazione.
lines.id: I want to bring something. It's how I was raised.
lines.literal: I-want to-bring something. is the my upbringing.

lines.speaker: Marco:
lines.text: Allora porta il vino. Ma non devi portare tutto il negozio!
lines.id: Then bring the wine. But don't bring the whole store!
lines.literal: then bring the wine. but not you-must to-bring all the store!

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: I promise. See you Saturday, then!

notes: **All three are followed by an infinitive.** *Posso venire*, *devo studiare*, *voglio portare* — the second verb doesn't change at all. Good news: only the first verb needs to be learned in all its forms.

**Non devo isn't "I mustn't".** *Non devo portare niente* means "I don't need to bring anything". For "mustn't", use *non posso* or *non si può*. This difference causes misunderstandings that are not funny.
**Vorrei is the soft form of voglio.** You've been using it since unit 4. Now it's clear where it comes from: it's the polite form of *volere*. When asking for something, always choose *vorrei*.
**Dai! means "come on".** One of the most frequent words in Italian conversation, used to coax, encourage, or show disbelief. It sounds like English "dye", one syllable.
**Saying no politely has its own pattern.** *Vorrei tanto, ma non posso* — first say you'd like to, then the obstacle. A bare *no, non posso* sounds cold by Italian standards.
**Verso le otto** = "around eight". *Verso* softens a time, and Italians use it constantly. In practice, *verso le otto* means between eight and eight-thirty.
**Niente and nulla both mean "nothing"**, and both need *non* before the verb: *non porto niente*. This double negative is required, just like *non… mai* in unit 7.
**Se vuoi** = "if you want". The formal version is *se vuole*. A gentle way to leave the choice to someone, a partner to *come vuoi* from unit 4.

grammars.title: Three helper verbs
body: All three are irregular and all three are essential. Notice the shared pattern: the *noi* and *voi* forms are always the most regular.
after: *Può* has an accent; without it the word doesn't exist. The same goes for *può darsi* (maybe), a common expression.
The soft forms of all three: *potrei* (could I), *dovrei* (I should), *vorrei* (I'd like). They're B1 level, but *vorrei* is a must right now.

grammars.title: When to use which
after: *Si può* and *non si può* mean "it's allowed" and "it's not allowed" in general, without saying who. Italian signs often read like this: *Non si può parcheggiare qui.*

blocks.title: Inviting
items: *Vuoi venire con me?* — Do you want to come with me?
*Andiamo a bere qualcosa?* — Shall we grab a drink?
*Ti va di andare al cinema?* — Do you feel like going to the movies?
*Che ne dici di sabato?* — How about Saturday?

blocks.title: Declining politely
items: *Mi dispiace, ma non posso.* — I'm sorry, but I can't.
*Vorrei tanto, ma devo lavorare.* — I'd love to, but I have to work.
*Purtroppo ho già un impegno.* — Unfortunately I already have plans.

blocks.text: *Magari* is a very hard Italian word to translate. It can mean "maybe", "if only", or — said on its own with a sigh — "I wish!". If someone answers your invitation with *magari!*, they'd really love to but can't.

items: I don't need to pay, it's already free. ____ pagare.

You don't need to bring anything. ____ portare niente.
You can't smoke here. Qui ____ fumare.
We don't need to get up early on Sundays. La domenica ____ alzarci presto.
